title: CUET Computer Science Test 13
subject: Computer Science / Informatics Practices
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Computer Science - 308.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: CUET (UG) 2025 308 paper structure and formats (no questions copied)
instructions: Attempt all 15 questions of Section A.
Then attempt all 35 questions of EITHER Section B1 (Computer Science) OR Section B2 (Informatics Practices) — 50 questions in total.
Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.

sections.title: Section A — Database Concepts, SQL and Computer Networks (compulsory)

questions.question: Table TRIP has a column City with the values Goa, Ooty, Goa, Leh, Ooty, Goa, Agra. How many rows are returned by SELECT DISTINCT City FROM TRIP; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4
Given: DISTINCT removes repeated values.
Step 1: Goa, Ooty, Leh, Agra → 4
Common mistake: (B) keeps duplicates. (C) and (D) miss cities.
Key point: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row.

questions.question: Table P has a column Name with the values Neha, Arjun, Zubin, Mira. What is the output of SELECT MAX(Name), MIN(Name) FROM P; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Zubin, Arjun
Given: Text is compared alphabetically.
Step 1: Order: Arjun, Mira, Neha, Zubin
Step 2: MAX = Zubin; MIN = Arjun
Common mistake: (A) takes the first and last rows. (C) swaps MAX and MIN. (D) has no basis.
Key point: MAX/MIN on dates give the latest/earliest date.

questions.question: Table T has 15 rows, none with City = 'Leh'. What is the output of SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(Marks) FROM T WHERE City = 'Leh'; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0, NULL
Given: No rows reach the aggregates.
Step 1: COUNT(*) of no rows = 0
Step 2: AVG of no values = NULL
Common mistake: (A) makes COUNT NULL. (B) makes AVG 0. (D) counts all rows.
Key point: Without GROUP BY, one result row is still returned.

questions.sub_topic: Rows from a product of two tables
questions.question: Table A has 6 rows and table B has 3 rows. How many rows does SELECT * FROM A, B; return?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 18
Given: Every row of A pairs with every row of B.
Step 1: 6 × 3 = 18
Common mistake: (A) adds. (B) and (C) take one table.
Key point: Add a join condition to avoid this.

questions.sub_topic: σ then π on Sales employees
questions.question: Relation EMP has 7 attributes and 50 tuples. Exactly 12 employees work in Sales, and no two of them share the same (Name, Salary). What are the degree and cardinality of π Name, Salary (σ Dept = 'Sales' (EMP))?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Degree 2, cardinality 12
Given: σ picks the 12 Sales tuples; π keeps 2 attributes.
Step 1: Degree = 2
Step 2: Cardinality = 12
Common mistake: (A) ignores π. (C) ignores σ. (D) swaps the two.
Key point: The order σ then π matters only for which tuples remain.

questions.question:
Match each expression (List-I) with its output (List-II):

List-I
(A) UCASE('Computer')
(B) LENGTH('Computer')
(C) LEFT('Computer', 4)
(D) INSTR('Computer', 'put')

List-II
(I) 4
(II) Comp
(III) 8
(IV) COMPUTER
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: UCASE gives COMPUTER (IV); there are 8 letters (III); the first 4 are 'Comp' (II); 'put' starts at position 4 (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps UCASE and LENGTH; (B) swaps LENGTH and LEFT; (C) swaps LEFT and INSTR.
Key point: INSTR() returns a position; LEFT() returns text.

questions.question:
A column Q has the values 12, 7, 20 and 5. Arrange the outputs of these functions in INCREASING order:
(A) COUNT(Q)
(B) MIN(Q)
(C) AVG(Q)
(D) MAX(Q)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B), (C), (D)
Why: COUNT = 4; MIN = 5; AVG = 44 ÷ 4 = 11; MAX = 20. So 4, 5, 11, 20.
Why not the others: (B) puts 5 before 4. (C) puts 11 before 5. (D) puts 11 before 4.
Key point: COUNT counts values; the others use the values themselves.

questions.sub_topic: Candidate keys of a CAR table
questions.question: Table CAR has the columns RegNo, EngineNo, Colour and Owner. Every car has a unique registration number and a unique engine number; colours and owners can repeat. Which are candidate keys?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) RegNo and EngineNo
Why: Candidate keys are attributes that can uniquely identify each tuple. RegNo and EngineNo are both unique for every car.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) include attributes that can repeat.
Key point: One candidate key becomes the primary key; the other is an alternate key.

questions.question: Relation STAFF has 8 tuples whose Dept values are HR, IT, HR, Sales, IT, IT, HR, Admin. How many tuples are in π Dept (STAFF)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4
Given: Projection keeps one attribute and removes duplicate tuples.
Step 1: Distinct departments: HR, IT, Sales, Admin → 4
Common mistake: (A) keeps duplicates. (B) and (D) miss departments.
Key point: SELECT DISTINCT Dept gives the same result.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Internet is a worldwide network of networks.
(B) The WWW is a service that runs on the Internet.
(C) E-mail uses the Internet but is not part of the WWW.
(D) The WWW existed before the Internet.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The Internet connects networks worldwide (A); the WWW, a system of linked web pages, is one of its services (B), and e-mail is another separate service (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the Internet grew from ARPANET (1969); the WWW came in 1990. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Internet ≠ WWW.

questions.question: Which device decides the path for data between DIFFERENT networks using IP addresses?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Router
Why: A router connects networks and forwards packets towards their destination network.
Why not the others: (B) forwards inside one LAN using MAC addresses. (C) broadcasts inside a LAN. (D) regenerates signals.
Key point: A home Wi-Fi router joins the home LAN to the ISP.

questions.sub_topic: Component needed on a wired LAN
questions.question: Every computer on a wired LAN needs which component to connect to the network cable?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Network interface card (NIC)
Why: The NIC (Ethernet card) connects a computer to the network and has a unique MAC address.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are separate devices with other roles.
Key point: Wireless NICs connect to Wi-Fi.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT LEFT('CHENNAI', 3), RIGHT('CHENNAI', 3); ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) CHE, NAI
Given: LEFT takes characters from the start; RIGHT from the end.
Step 1: LEFT('CHENNAI', 3) = 'CHE'
Step 2: RIGHT('CHENNAI', 3) = 'NAI'
Common mistake: (A) uses LEFT twice. (B) swaps them. (D) takes 4 characters.
Key point: Both count characters, not positions.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The domain of the attribute Gender in a STUDENT relation may be {M, F, T}.
Reason (R): A domain is the set of values that an attribute is allowed to take.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Since a domain lists the permitted values of an attribute, {M, F, T} can be the domain of Gender. The Reason explains the Assertion.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both are true.
Key point: All values in a column come from its domain.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT LENGTH(LTRIM('   SQL')); ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3
Given: LTRIM() removes leading spaces.
Step 1: '   SQL' → 'SQL'
Step 2: LENGTH('SQL') = 3
Common mistake: (A) counts the spaces. (C) assumes all is removed. (D) miscounts.
Key point: RTRIM() would have no effect here.

questions.question: In binary search on an ascending list, if L[mid] > key, which statement should run next?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) high = mid - 1
Why: If the middle element is larger than the key, the key can only be in the left half, so the upper limit moves to mid − 1.
Why not the others: (B) searches the wrong half. (C) and (D) move the limits in the wrong direction.
Key point: The search stops when low > high.

questions.question:
Fill in the blank in this insertion sort:

for i in range(1, len(L)):
    t = L[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and L[j] > t:
        L[j + 1] = L[j]
        j -= 1
    ________
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) L[j + 1] = t
Why: After shifting larger elements right, the gap is at index j + 1, where the saved element must be placed.
Why not the others: (A) overwrites the element before the gap. (B) puts it back where it started. (D) loses the saved value.
Key point: The loop stops when a smaller element or the start is reached.

questions.question: What is [7, 2, 9, 4, 1] after the FIRST pass of bubble sort (ascending)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) [2, 7, 4, 1, 9]
Given: Adjacent pairs are compared and swapped if out of order.
Step 1: (7,2) swap → [2, 7, 9, 4, 1]; (7,9) no
Step 2: (9,4) swap → [2, 7, 4, 9, 1]; (9,1) swap → [2, 7, 4, 1, 9]
Common mistake: (A) stops before the last comparison. (C) is sorted. (D) does part of pass 2.
Key point: The largest value reaches the end.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

def f():
    try:
        return 'T'
    finally:
        print('F')

print(f())
options: A) T then F (on separate lines)
B) F then T (on separate lines)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) F then T (on separate lines)
Given: finally runs before the function actually returns.
Step 1: return 'T' is reached, but before leaving f(), finally prints F
Step 2: Then print(f()) prints the returned value T
Common mistake: (A) assumes return happens first. (C) forgets finally. (D) forgets the returned value.
Key point: finally runs even when try contains return.

questions.question:
With h(k) = k % 7, match each key (List-I) with its slot (List-II):

List-I
(A) 15
(B) 23
(C) 40
(D) 34

List-II
(I) 6
(II) 5
(III) 2
(IV) 1
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: 15 % 7 = 1 (IV); 23 % 7 = 2 (III); 40 % 7 = 5 (II); 34 % 7 = 6 (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps 15 and 23; (B) swaps 23 and 40; (D) swaps 40 and 34.
Key point: No two of these keys collide.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question: A 60 MB file is downloaded over a 12 Mbps connection. Ignoring delays and taking 1 byte = 8 bits, about how long does it take?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 40 seconds
Given: 60 MB = 480 Mb.
Step 1: 480 ÷ 12 = 40 seconds
Common mistake: (A) forgets bits. (C) multiplies. (D) has no basis.
Key point: File sizes use bytes; speeds use bits.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pickle
with open('p.dat', 'wb') as g:
    for i in range(4):
        pickle.dump(i * i, g)
c, t = 0, 0
with open('p.dat', 'rb') as g:
    try:
        while True:
            t += pickle.load(g)
            c += 1
    except EOFError:
        pass
print(c, t)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4 14
Given: The dumped values are 0, 1, 4 and 9.
Step 1: Four loads succeed → c = 4
Step 2: t = 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14; the fifth load raises EOFError, which ends the loop
Common mistake: (B) misses the 0. (C) uses squares up to 4. (D) adds 0 + 1 + 2 + 3.
Key point: EOFError is the normal signal that the file has ended.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question:
Arrange the following data transfer rates in INCREASING order:
(A) 1 Tbps
(B) 1 Gbps
(C) 1 Kbps
(D) 1 Mbps
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: Kbps < Mbps < Gbps < Tbps, each 1024 times the previous one.
Why not the others: (A) is decreasing. (B) puts Mbps before Kbps. (D) puts Gbps before Mbps.
Key point: The prefixes are kilo, mega, giga and tera.

questions.sub_topic: WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING with ORDER BY
questions.question:
Table ORD has these (Cust, Amt) rows: (Ravi, 400), (Sana, 150), (Ravi, 300), (Tom, 700), (Sana, 500), (Tom, 100). What is the output of:

SELECT Cust, SUM(Amt) FROM ORD WHERE Amt > 120 GROUP BY Cust HAVING SUM(Amt) >= 650 ORDER BY SUM(Amt);
options: A) Sana 650, Ravi 700, Tom 700 — in that order
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Sana 650, Ravi 700, Tom 700 — in that order
Given: WHERE removes Tom's 100 first.
Step 1: Ravi 400 + 300 = 700; Sana 150 + 500 = 650; Tom 700
Step 2: All three have SUM ≥ 650
Step 3: Ascending by SUM: Sana 650, then Ravi and Tom at 700
Common mistake: (B) keeps Tom's 100. (C) sorts in descending order. (D) drops Tom.
Key point: Rows with equal sums may appear in any order unless another sort column is given.

questions.question:
Monthly sales (₹ thousand) of three shops:

Shop | Jan | Feb | Mar
P | 40 | 45 | 50
Q | 55 | 35 | 40
R | 30 | 60 | 52

Which shop had the highest total sales over the three months?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) R
Given: Add each shop's three months.
Step 1: P = 40 + 45 + 50 = 135; Q = 55 + 35 + 40 = 130
Step 2: R = 30 + 60 + 52 = 142 → highest
Common mistake: (A) is second. (B) has the highest January sales only. (D) The totals differ.
Key point: Always total before comparing.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a data set:
(A) Adding 5 to every value increases the mean by 5.
(B) Adding 5 to every value leaves the standard deviation unchanged.
(C) Multiplying every value by 2 doubles the standard deviation.
(D) Multiplying every value by 2 leaves the mean unchanged.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: A constant shift moves the mean (A) but not the spread (B); scaling by 2 stretches all deviations, doubling the SD (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — the mean also doubles. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: Shifts change the centre; scaling changes both centre and spread.

Answer: (D) 3 5
Given: c counts the comparisons made.
Step 1: Key 7 is found at the 3rd comparison → 3
Step 2: Key 5 is absent → all 5 compared → 5
Common mistake: (A) and (C) return the index instead of the count. (B) returns 0 for 'not found'.
Key point: An unsuccessful linear search compares every element.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(A) Circuit switching
(B) Packet switching
(C) Simplex
(D) Full-duplex

List-II
(I) Mobile phone conversation
(II) FM radio broadcast
(III) Data sent in pieces that may take different routes, as on the Internet
(IV) A dedicated path for the whole call, as in a landline call
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Circuit switching reserves a path (IV); packet switching sends independent packets (III); simplex is one-way (II); full-duplex is both ways at once (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two switching types; (B) swaps packet switching and simplex; (C) swaps simplex and full-duplex.
Key point: The Internet uses packet switching.

questions.question:
For a hash table using h(k) = k % n, consider the following statements:
(A) The table needs n slots, numbered 0 to n − 1.
(B) Two keys with the same remainder cause a collision.
(C) The table can have fewer than n slots without any problem.
(D) The keys must be sorted before they are hashed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A) and (B) only
Why: Remainders range from 0 to n − 1, needing n slots (A); equal remainders collide (B).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — a remainder could point beyond the table. Statement (D) is false — hashing does not need sorting. Options (A), (C) and (D) include one or both.
Key point: Choosing n well reduces collisions.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) SELECT 5 + NULL; returns NULL.
(B) IS NULL is used to find missing values.
(C) COUNT(*) skips rows that contain NULL.
(D) AVG() ignores NULL values.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL (A); IS NULL tests for it (B); aggregates such as AVG skip it (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — COUNT(*) counts every row. Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: COUNT(column) skips NULLs.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.sub_topic: Counting lines including a blank line
questions.question:
r.txt contains: 'one\n', 'two\n', '\n' (a blank line) and 'four\n'. What is printed?

f = open('r.txt')
n = 0
while True:
    line = f.readline()
    if not line:
        break
    n += 1
print(n)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4
Given: A blank line is read as '\n', which is not empty; only the end of the file gives ''.
Step 1: Four lines are read, including the blank one → n = 4
Common mistake: (A) skips the blank line. (B) and (D) miscount.
Key point: line.strip() == '' would detect blank lines.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): When evaluating 8 2 − with a stack, the first value popped (2) is used as the RIGHT operand.
Reason (R): A stack is LIFO, so the operand pushed last (2) is popped first.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: 8 is pushed, then 2; popping gives 2 first, then 8, so the operation is 8 − 2 = 6. The Reason explains why the first popped value is the right operand.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both are true.
Key point: Reversing the operands would give 2 − 8 = −6.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) An absolute path starts from the root folder of the drive.
(B) A relative path is given from the current working folder.
(C) '..' in a path means the parent folder.
(D) Relative paths work only on Windows.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: NCERT explains absolute paths (from the root) (A), relative paths (from the current folder) (B), and '..' for the parent folder (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — relative paths work on all operating systems. Options (A), (B) and (C) include it.
Key point: Use relative paths so programs work in any folder.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question:
Assertion (A): In packet switching, the packets of one message may arrive at the destination out of order.
Reason (R): In packet switching, a dedicated path is reserved for the whole message.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
Why: The Assertion is true — packets travel independently and may take different routes. The Reason is false — reserving a dedicated path is circuit switching.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) need a true Reason. (D) The Assertion is true.
Key point: The receiver reassembles packets using their sequence information.

questions.sub_topic: FIFO order of P, Q, R, S
questions.question:
Customers P, Q, R and S join an empty queue in that order. Arrange them in the order in which they are served:
(A) P
(B) Q
(C) R
(D) S
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B), (C), (D)
Why: A queue is FIFO: the first to join is the first served.
Why not the others: (B) is LIFO (a stack). (C) and (D) mix the order.
Key point: Compare with a stack, which reverses the order.

questions.question: What is the postfix form of (A − B) / (C + D * E) ?
options: A) A B − C D + E * /
B) A B C D E − + * /
C) A B − / C D E * +
D) A B − C D E * + /
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A B − C D E * + /
Given: Convert each bracket; * before + inside the second bracket.
Step 1: (A − B) → A B −
Step 2: (C + D * E) → C D E * +
Step 3: Divide: A B − C D E * + /
Common mistake: (A) adds C and D first. (B) loses the grouping. (C) places / too early.
Key point: The main operator (/) comes last.

questions.question:
Match each postfix expression (List-I) with its value (List-II):

List-I
(A) 2 3 +
(B) 6 2 /
(C) 4 2 3 * +
(D) 5 1 2 + *

List-II
(I) 15
(II) 10
(III) 3
(IV) 5
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: 2 + 3 = 5 (IV); 6 / 2 = 3 (III); 4 + 2 × 3 = 10 (II); 5 × (1 + 2) = 15 (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Each operator works on the two values just before it.

questions.question: Which statement creates a table where RollNo is the primary key and Name cannot be left empty?
options: A) CREATE TABLE S (RollNo INT, Name VARCHAR(20)) PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL;
B) CREATE S TABLE (RollNo INT PRIMARY, Name NOT NULL);
C) CREATE TABLE S (RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
D) CREATE TABLE S (RollNo PRIMARY KEY INT, Name VARCHAR NOT NULL(20));
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) CREATE TABLE S (RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
Why: Constraints are written after each column's data type: RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL.
Why not the others: (A) places constraints outside the column list. (B) and (D) have wrong syntax.
Key point: Table-level PRIMARY KEY(RollNo) is also allowed.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.question:
Match each block (List-I) with when it runs (List-II):

List-I
(A) try
(B) except
(C) else
(D) finally

List-II
(I) Always, whether or not an exception occurs
(II) Only if no exception occurs in try
(III) Only if a matching exception occurs
(IV) First, with the code that might raise an exception
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: try holds the risky code (IV); except runs on a matching error (III); else runs when there is no error (II); finally always runs (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps try and except; (C) swaps except and else; (D) swaps else and finally.
Key point: else and finally are optional.

questions.question: q = ['A', 'B'] (front at index 0). After q.append('C'), q.pop(0), q.append('D') and q.pop(0), what is q?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ['C', 'D']
Given: append adds at the rear; pop(0) removes the front.
Step 1: [A, B, C] → remove A → [B, C]
Step 2: [B, C, D] → remove B → [C, D]
Common mistake: (A) ignores all operations. (C) removes C instead of B. (D) removes from the rear.
Key point: FIFO — the earliest element leaves first.

questions.sub_topic: Serving two customers at a time
questions.question:
Customers 1 to 7 join a queue one per minute. Whenever a customer whose number is a multiple of 3 joins, two customers are served from the front. What are the queue and the served list after customer 7 joins?

q, served = [], []
for t in range(1, 8):
    q.append(t)
    if t % 3 == 0:
        served.append(q.pop(0))
        served.append(q.pop(0))
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) q = [5, 6, 7], served = [1, 2, 3, 4]
Given: Service happens at t = 3 and t = 6.
Step 1: t = 3: [1, 2, 3] → serve 1, 2 → [3]
Step 2: t = 6: [3, 4, 5, 6] → serve 3, 4 → [5, 6]
Step 3: t = 7: [5, 6, 7]
Common mistake: (A) serves one extra. (B) skips customer 3. (D) serves everyone.
Key point: Simulations like this model ticket counters and printers.

questions.question: Insertion sort (ascending) is applied to [6, 3, 8, 2, 5]. What is the list after the elements at indices 1, 2 and 3 have been inserted?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) [2, 3, 6, 8, 5]
Given: Each step inserts one element into the sorted part.
Step 1: Insert 3 → [3, 6, 8, 2, 5]; insert 8 → unchanged
Step 2: Insert 2 → shift 8, 6, 3 → [2, 3, 6, 8, 5]
Common mistake: (A) is after two insertions. (B) is fully sorted. (C) also moves 5.
Key point: The last element, 5, is inserted in the next pass.

questions.question: What is the median of 33, 21, 45, 18, 27, 39, 24?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 27
Given: Seven values → the 4th value after sorting.
Step 1: Sorted: 18, 21, 24, 27, 33, 39, 45
Step 2: 4th value = 27
Common mistake: (B) is the mean. (C) is the minimum. (D) is the 6th value.
Key point: With an odd count, the median is a data value.

questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

s = []
s.append('a')
s.append('b')
s.pop()
s.append('c')
s.append('d')
s.pop()
print(s)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ['a', 'c']
Given: Each pop() removes the top element.
Step 1: [a, b] → pop b → [a]
Step 2: [a, c, d] → pop d → [a, c]
Common mistake: (A) pops the wrong element. (B) pops from the bottom. (D) pops c instead of d.
Key point: The top is the most recently pushed element.

questions.question: Table T has a column Code with the values A12, B7, A9, AB3, A105. How many rows are returned by SELECT * FROM T WHERE Code LIKE 'A__'; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2
Given: 'A__' means A followed by exactly two characters.
Step 1: A12 (3 characters) and AB3 (3 characters) match
Step 2: A9 has 2 characters; A105 has 4; B7 does not start with A
Common mistake: (A) also counts A9 or A105. (C) treats _ as %. (D) misses AB3.
Key point: _ matches exactly one character.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

One Monday, the computers in a school lab became very slow. Investigation showed:
1. A student had opened an e-mail attachment named results.exe. The malicious code attached itself to other program files on that computer and spread whenever those files were run or copied.
2. Overnight, another malicious program copied itself across the lab network to every computer, without anyone opening a file.
3. The school website could not be opened, because thousands of requests were arriving every second from many different computers around the world.
4. The IT head then set rules on the school's firewall, updated the antivirus software on all computers and restored files from the last backup.

Question: The code from results.exe attached itself to other program files and spread when they were run or copied. This malware is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Virus
Given: It needs a host file to spread.
Step 1: Malware that attaches to host files is a virus
Common mistake: (B) spreads on its own. (C) is a text file. (D) is a protection.
Key point: Opening unknown .exe attachments is risky.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

One Monday, the computers in a school lab became very slow. Investigation showed:
1. A student had opened an e-mail attachment named results.exe. The malicious code attached itself to other program files on that computer and spread whenever those files were run or copied.

4. The IT head then set rules on the school's firewall, updated the antivirus software on all computers and restored files from the last backup.

Question: The program that copied itself across the network to every computer without anyone opening a file is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Worm
Given: It spread by itself over the network.
Step 1: Self-replicating, network-spreading malware is a worm
Common mistake: (A) disguises itself as useful software. (B) needs a host file. (C) is unwanted e-mail.
Key point: Worms can consume network bandwidth.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

One Monday, the computers in a school lab became very slow. Investigation showed:
1. A student had opened an e-mail attachment named results.exe. The malicious code attached itself to other program files on that computer and spread whenever those files were run or copied.
2. Overnight, another malicious program copied itself across the lab network to every computer, without anyone opening a file.

4. The IT head then set rules on the school's firewall, updated the antivirus software on all computers and restored files from the last backup.

Question: The website could not be opened because of requests from many computers around the world. This attack is a:
options: A) A phishing attack using fake e-mails
B) A Distributed Denial of Service attack
C) An eavesdropping attack on calls
D) A case of plagiarism of web content
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A Distributed Denial of Service attack
Given: Many sources overloaded the server.
Step 1: Overloading from many computers is a DDoS attack
Common mistake: (A) steals details using fake messages. (C) listens to communication. (D) is copying work.
Key point: DoS attacks target availability.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

One Monday, the computers in a school lab became very slow. Investigation showed:
1. A student had opened an e-mail attachment named results.exe. The malicious code attached itself to other program files on that computer and spread whenever those files were run or copied.
2. Overnight, another malicious program copied itself across the lab network to every computer, without anyone opening a file.
3. The school website could not be opened, because thousands of requests were arriving every second from many different computers around the world.
4. The IT head then set rules on the school's firewall, updated the antivirus software on all computers and restored files from the last backup.

Question: What do the firewall rules set by the IT head mainly do?
options: A) It removes the virus from all infected files
B) It allows or blocks traffic using set rules
C) It restores the files that were deleted
D) It speeds up the processors of the computers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It allows or blocks traffic using set rules
Given: A firewall monitors traffic between networks.
Step 1: It filters traffic using rules, blocking suspicious connections
Common mistake: (A) is antivirus work. (C) is done by backups. (D) is not a firewall's job.
Key point: Firewalls and antivirus software work together.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

One Monday, the computers in a school lab became very slow. Investigation showed:
1. A student had opened an e-mail attachment named results.exe. The malicious code attached itself to other program files on that computer and spread whenever those files were run or copied.
2. Overnight, another malicious program copied itself across the lab network to every computer, without anyone opening a file.
3. The school website could not be opened, because thousands of requests were arriving every second from many different computers around the world.
4. The IT head then set rules on the school's firewall, updated the antivirus software on all computers and restored files from the last backup.

Question: Which statement about this incident is NOT correct?
options: A) Updated antivirus software can detect and remove known viruses and worms
B) Restoring from a backup can recover files damaged by malware
C) Not opening unknown attachments could have prevented the first infection
D) The firewall alone would have cleaned the virus from the infected program files
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The firewall alone would have cleaned the virus from the infected program files
Given: Each measure does a different job.
Step 1: A firewall filters network traffic; it does not scan or clean infected files
Common mistake: (A), (B) and (C) are correct lessons from the incident.
Key point: Security works in layers: firewall, antivirus, backups and safe habits.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
For s = pd.Series([1.5, 2.5], index=['p', 'q']), match each attribute (List-I) with its value (List-II):

List-I
(A) s.dtype
(B) s.values
(C) s.index
(D) s.size

List-II
(I) 2
(II) Index(['p', 'q'])
(III) array([1.5, 2.5])
(IV) float64
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: dtype is float64 (IV); values is the NumPy array (III); index holds the labels (II); size is 2 (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps dtype and values; (B) swaps values and index; (D) swaps index and size.
Key point: s.empty would be False.

questions.question: Which statement makes the x-axis label larger?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) plt.xlabel('Month', fontsize=14)
Why: fontsize sets the size of label and title text.
Why not the others: (B) width is not a label option. (C) sets tick labels incorrectly. (D) show() takes no size.
Key point: color can also be given to labels.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
d1 = pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2]})
d2 = pd.DataFrame({'a': [3], 'b': [4]})
c = pd.concat([d1, d2])
print(c.shape, c['b'].isnull().sum())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (3, 2) 2
Given: Rows are stacked; columns are the union a, b.
Step 1: Shape = (3, 2)
Step 2: d1's two rows have no b → 2 NaN
Common mistake: (A) drops column b. (B) loses a row. (C) forgets the missing values.
Key point: Missing columns are filled with NaN.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question:
Arrange the steps to display the three students with the highest total marks from marks.csv:
(A) df = pd.read_csv('marks.csv')
(B) df['Total'] = df['Eng'] + df['Maths'] + df['Sci']
(C) df = df.sort_values('Total', ascending=False)
(D) print(df.head(3))
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B), (C), (D)
Why: Read (A), compute totals (B), sort from highest (C), and show the first three (D).
Why not the others: (A) computes before reading. (B) sorts before Total exists. (C) prints before sorting.
Key point: nlargest(3, 'Total') is a shortcut.

questions.question: Table T has a column Name with the values Ira, Kabir, Om and Shreya. What is the output of SELECT MAX(LENGTH(Name)) FROM T; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6
Given: LENGTH() works on each row; MAX() takes the largest result.
Step 1: Lengths: 3, 5, 2, 6
Step 2: MAX = 6
Common mistake: (A) is Kabir's length. (B) has no basis. (D) returns the name, not the length.
Key point: A single-row function can be inside an aggregate.

questions.question:
Arrange the steps a team follows to make and use a project timeline:
(A) Track progress against the deadlines
(B) Estimate how long each task will take
(C) List all the tasks of the project
(D) Assign a deadline and a member to each task
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: List tasks (C), estimate their time (B), assign deadlines and owners (D), then track progress (A).
Why not the others: (A) assigns deadlines before estimating time. (B) estimates before listing tasks. (D) tracks before deadlines exist.
Key point: Update the timeline when delays happen.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT MOD(YEAR('2025-12-31'), 100); ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 25
Given: YEAR() = 2025.
Step 1: 2025 = 20 × 100 + 25 → MOD = 25
Common mistake: (B) gives the quotient. (C) uses MONTH(). (D) uses DAY().
Key point: MOD(x, 100) gives the last two digits.

questions.sub_topic: Reading a line chart of temperatures
questions.question: A line chart shows the temperature (°C) at 6 a.m., 9 a.m., 12 noon, 3 p.m. and 6 p.m.: 18, 24, 31, 33, 27. Between which two consecutive readings did the temperature rise the most?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 9 a.m. and 12 noon
Given: Differences: +6, +7, +2, −6.
Step 1: The largest rise, +7, is from 9 a.m. to 12 noon
Common mistake: (A) is +2. (C) is +6. (D) is a fall.
Key point: The steepest upward segment shows the largest rise.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) plt.title() sets the heading of the chart.
(B) plt.ylabel() names the y-axis.
(C) plt.legend() works even if no line has a label, showing all lines.
(D) plt.xlabel() must be called before plt.plot().
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A) and (B) only
Why: title() and ylabel() work as described (A, B).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — without labels, legend() has nothing to show. Statement (D) is false — labels can be set before or after plotting, as long as it is before show(). Options (A), (C) and (D) include one or both.
Key point: Call show() last.

questions.question:
Match each expression (List-I) with its output (List-II):

List-I
(A) ROUND(15.678, 2)
(B) ROUND(15.678)
(C) ROUND(15.678, -1)
(D) ROUND(15.678, 1)

List-II
(I) 15.7
(II) 20
(III) 16
(IV) 15.68
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Two places → 15.68 (IV); no places → 16 (III); −1 → nearest ten, 20 (II); one place → 15.7 (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: A negative argument rounds to the left of the decimal point.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
a = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=['x', 'y', 'z'])
b = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], index=['y', 'z', 'w'])
print((a + b).dropna().tolist())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) [21.0, 32.0]
Given: Values are added label by label; labels in only one Series give NaN.
Step 1: y → 20 + 1 = 21; z → 30 + 2 = 32; x and w → NaN
Step 2: dropna() removes the NaN values → [21.0, 32.0]
Common mistake: (B) adds by position. (C) forgets dropna(). (D) treats missing as 0.
Key point: a.add(b, fill_value=0) would treat missing values as 0.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question: A DataFrame has the columns Name, City and Marks. Which columns does df.describe() summarise by default?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Marks only
Why: By default, describe() summarises only numeric columns.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) need include='all' for text columns. (D) Marks is numeric.
Key point: For text, describe() reports count, unique, top and freq.

questions.question: A program calls plt.plot(a, label='Delhi'), plt.plot(b, label='Pune'), plt.plot(c) and plt.plot(d, label='Goa'), then plt.legend(). How many entries does the legend show?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3
Given: Only labelled lines appear in the legend.
Step 1: Delhi, Pune and Goa have labels; the third line has none → 3 entries
Common mistake: (A) counts the unlabelled line. (B) and (D) miscount.
Key point: Use label= for every line you want in the legend.

questions.question:
Match each e-mail field (List-I) with its use (List-II):

List-I
(A) To
(B) Cc
(C) Bcc
(D) Attachment

List-II
(I) A file sent along with the message
(II) Recipients whose addresses are hidden from others
(III) Recipients who get a copy, visible to everyone
(IV) The main recipients
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: To holds the main recipients (IV); Cc sends visible copies (III); Bcc sends hidden copies (II); an attachment is a file (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps To and Cc; (B) swaps Cc and Bcc; (C) swaps Bcc and attachment.
Key point: Large attachments may be blocked by mail servers.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
k = pd.DataFrame({'N': list('pqrs'), 'G': ['X', 'Y', 'X', 'Y'], 'M': [70, 85, 90, 60]})
print(k.sort_values(['G', 'M'], ascending=[False, True])['N'].tolist())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ['s', 'q', 'p', 'r']
Given: G descending (Y before X); within each group, M ascending.
Step 1: G = Y: s (60), q (85) → s, q
Step 2: G = X: p (70), r (90) → p, r
Common mistake: (A) sorts G ascending. (C) sorts M descending. (D) reverses both.
Key point: ascending takes one value per sort column.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question: Which library provides the Series and DataFrame data structures?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Pandas
Why: Pandas, built on NumPy, provides Series and DataFrames for data analysis.
Why not the others: (A) plots. (C) is a DBMS. (D) serialises objects.
Key point: import pandas as pd is the usual import.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question: For s = pd.Series([15, 42, 8, 27, 33]), what is s[s > 20].tolist()?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) [42, 27, 33]
Given: s > 20 gives a True/False mask.
Step 1: 42, 27, 33 are greater than 20
Common mistake: (A) keeps values ≤ 20. (B) misses 27. (D) shows a wrong mask.
Key point: Boolean indexing keeps the original labels.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question: For the same s, what is s.tail(2).tolist()?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) [27, 33]
Given: tail(2) gives the last two elements.
Step 1: 27 and 33
Common mistake: (A) is head(2). (B) is tail(3). (C) is tail(1).
Key point: tail() defaults to 5 elements.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) NOW() returns the current date and time.
(B) DATE(NOW()) returns only the current date.
(C) MONTH('2025-03-01') returns 'March'.
(D) DAYNAME() returns the name of the weekday.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: NOW() gives date and time (A); DATE() extracts the date (B); DAYNAME() gives names such as 'Monday' (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — MONTH() returns the number 3; MONTHNAME() returns 'March'. Options (A), (B) and (C) include it.
Key point: Number-returning and name-returning date functions are different.

questions.sub_topic: Plotting a column read from a file
questions.question: After df = pd.read_csv('rain.csv'), which statement draws a bar chart of the Rainfall column against the Month column?
options: C) plt.bar(df) with no other arguments
D) plt.hist(df) for the whole table
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) plt.bar(df['Month'], df['Rainfall'])
Why: plt.bar(x, height) needs the categories (Month) and the heights (Rainfall).
Why not the others: (D) draws a histogram of the whole frame. (B) draws a pie chart. (C) gives no x and height.
Key point: df.plot(kind='bar', x='Month', y='Rainfall') also works.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question: What is pd.Series([12, 5, 9, 20, 7, 15]).median()?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 10.5
Given: Sorted: 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20.
Step 1: Middle two: 9 and 12 → median = 10.5
Common mistake: (B) is the mean. (C) and (D) take one middle value.
Key point: median() skips NaN.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question:
For z = pd.Series([2, 8, 5, 5]), match each expression (List-I) with its value (List-II):

List-I
(A) z.sum()
(B) z.mean()
(C) z.max()
(D) z.count()

List-II
(I) 4
(II) 8
(III) 5.0
(IV) 20
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: sum = 20 (IV); mean = 5.0 (III); max = 8 (II); count = 4 (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps sum and mean; (C) swaps mean and max; (D) swaps max and count.
Key point: mode() would give 5.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A website that uses HTTPS can never be a phishing website.
Reason (R): HTTPS encrypts the data exchanged between the browser and the server.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: The Reason is true — HTTPS encrypts the connection. But the Assertion is false — encryption does not prove that a site is honest; criminals can also obtain certificates for fake look-alike sites.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) need a true Assertion.
Key point: Check the exact domain name, not just the padlock.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.sub_topic: List of dictionaries with different keys
questions.question:
What are x.shape and the total number of NaN values?

import pandas as pd
x = pd.DataFrame([{'n': 'A', 'm': 5}, {'n': 'B'}, {'m': 7, 'k': 1}])
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (3, 3) and 4
Given: Columns are the union of keys: n, m, k.
Step 1: Shape = (3 rows, 3 columns)
Step 2: Missing: row 0 lacks k (1); row 1 lacks m and k (2); row 2 lacks n (1) → 4
Common mistake: (A) ignores k. (C) swaps rows and columns. (D) misses one NaN.
Key point: Each dictionary becomes one row.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about for i, row in df.iterrows():
(A) i takes the index label of each row.
(B) row is a Series holding that row's values.
(C) row['Marks'] gives the Marks value of that row.
(D) iterrows() goes through the DataFrame column by column.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: iterrows() yields (label, row Series) pairs (A, B), so a column value is read by its label (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — iterrows() goes row by row; items() goes column by column. Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Vectorised operations are usually faster than loops.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about cookies:
(A) Cookies can keep a user logged in to a website.
(B) Cookies can remember items placed in a shopping cart.
(C) Cookies are programs that can delete files on the computer.
(D) Cookies can never be used to track users.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A) and (B) only
Why: Cookies store session and preference data such as login status (A) and cart items (B).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — cookies are small text files, not programs. Statement (D) is false — third-party cookies are used to track browsing. Options (A), (C) and (D) include one or both.
Key point: Browsers let users block third-party cookies.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): df['Marks'].plot(kind='hist') draws a histogram of the marks.
Reason (R): The kind argument of the Pandas plot() method selects the type of chart.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Setting kind='hist' tells plot() to draw a histogram. The Reason explains the Assertion.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both are true.
Key point: bins can also be passed to plot(kind='hist').

questions.question: Why does a website usually load faster the second time it is opened in the same browser?
options: A) The website's server becomes faster after each visit
B) The ISP doubles the speed for repeat visits
C) The browser reuses copies of images and files stored in its cache
D) Cookies make the network cable faster
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The browser reuses copies of images and files stored in its cache
Why: The cache stores copies of resources such as images and scripts, so the browser need not download them again.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are false.
Key point: Clearing the cache frees storage space.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question: For g = pd.DataFrame({'H': ['R', 'B', 'R', 'G', 'B'], 'S': [45, 60, 72, 55, 38]}), what is g.groupby('H')['S'].max().to_dict()?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) {'B': 60, 'G': 55, 'R': 72}
Given: max() is found inside each house.
Step 1: R: 45, 72 → 72; B: 60, 38 → 60; G: 55
Common mistake: (A) takes the first values. (B) gives sums. (C) gives only the overall maximum.
Key point: Groups appear in sorted key order.

questions.question: What is the output of SELECT LENGTH(TRIM('  AI  ')) * 2; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4
Given: TRIM('  AI  ') = 'AI'.
Step 1: LENGTH = 2; 2 × 2 = 4
Common mistake: (A) keeps the spaces. (B) removes spaces on one side. (C) forgets × 2.
Key point: Functions are evaluated from the inside out.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Karan, a Class 12 student, faced several problems in one month:
1. He received an SMS saying 'Your bank account will be blocked today. Update KYC here', with a link. The page looked exactly like his bank's website, and he typed his net-banking password.
2. The next day, someone used his bank details and identity to make online purchases in his name.
3. A classmate posted edited photos of Karan on social media with insulting comments, and kept sending him threatening messages.
4. Karan found that a stranger had copied his school project from his blog and was showing it as their own work on another website.

Question: The SMS with a link to a fake bank page that collected Karan's password is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Phishing
Given: A fake message and a look-alike website tricked him into giving his password.
Step 1: This is phishing (by SMS, sometimes called smishing)
Common mistake: (A) involves permission. (B) is copying work. (D) is provoking people online.
Key point: Banks never ask for passwords through links.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Karan, a Class 12 student, faced several problems in one month:
1. He received an SMS saying 'Your bank account will be blocked today. Update KYC here', with a link. The page looked exactly like his bank's website, and he typed his net-banking password.
2. The next day, someone used his bank details and identity to make online purchases in his name.
3. A classmate posted edited photos of Karan on social media with insulting comments, and kept sending him threatening messages.
4. Karan found that a stranger had copied his school project from his blog and was showing it as their own work on another website.

Question: Someone used Karan's bank details and identity to shop online. This crime is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Identity theft
Given: His personal details were used to impersonate him.
Step 1: Using another person's identity for gain is identity theft
Common mistake: (B) is harassment. (C) concerns creative works. (D) is bulk unwanted messages.
Key point: Monitor bank statements to spot misuse early.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Karan, a Class 12 student, faced several problems in one month:
1. He received an SMS saying 'Your bank account will be blocked today. Update KYC here', with a link. The page looked exactly like his bank's website, and he typed his net-banking password.
2. The next day, someone used his bank details and identity to make online purchases in his name.
3. A classmate posted edited photos of Karan on social media with insulting comments, and kept sending him threatening messages.
4. Karan found that a stranger had copied his school project from his blog and was showing it as their own work on another website.

Question: What should Karan do FIRST after realising that he typed his password on the fake page?
options: A) Wait a few days to see whether any money is taken
B) Forward the SMS to friends but not tell the bank
C) Contact the bank at once, change the password, report it
D) Delete the SMS and simply forget about the matter
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Contact the bank at once, change the password, report it
Given: The attacker may use the password at any moment.
Step 1: The bank must be told immediately so that the account can be secured
Step 2: Changing passwords and reporting the crime limit the damage
Common mistake: (A) and (D) allow more loss. (B) delays the urgent action.
Key point: Speed matters in cyber fraud cases.
